source_text: Nec aliena peccata aliis imputaret ac per hoc nec propter parentum iniquitates innocentes eorum filios, qui per se nihil operati essent vel boni vel mali, per quod parentum suorum crimina docerentur imitati, aeternis adiudicaret suppliciis [n4] . Quibus collectis Deum et esse et iustum esse constat, quem claruerat, si aliquid operetur iniustum, tantum subire in divinitate, quantum pertulisset in aequitate dispendium.
pass_a_gloss: Nor would he impute others' sins to others, and through this neither on account of parents' injustices would he adjudge to eternal punishments their innocent children, who through themselves had worked nothing either good or evil by which they would be shown to have imitated their parents' crimes. With these collected, it stands that God both is and is just, whom it had become clear, if he should work anything unjust, would undergo as much loss in divinity as he had suffered in fairness.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Nor would he charge some people with other people’s sins. Accordingly, he would not sentence innocent children to eternal punishment because of their parents’ wrongdoing, when those children had personally done nothing either good or evil by which they could be shown to have imitated their parents’ crimes. Taken together, these considerations establish both that God exists and that he is just. For it was clear that, if he did anything unjust, his divinity would suffer exactly as much damage as his fairness did.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Scripture's destruction of iniquitas is the Law's purpose; keep moral injustice.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: The children have done neither good nor evil.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
